newsitem.title: UK: Iraqi oil shipments may not resume until July-trade.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi oil shipments may not resume until July-trade.

text.p: The resumption of Iraqi crude exports under the terms of the United Nations oil-for-food deal renewed last week may be delayed until July as European lifters seek increased volumes and a new price formula, traders said on Monday.

Some European oil companies planning to buy Iraqi crude under the terms of the deal had been hoping for a speedy rollover of contracts covering the first 180 days but others have requested higher volumes and a new price formula for sales to northwest Europe, they said.
"There are a few companies asking for a new price for northwest Europe and that's taking a little time," said a source at a European oil company.
"Baghdad doesn't seem to be in a hurry to sign anything until everything is sorted out."

Traders said companies were asking Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) for the price formula for Kirkuk Blend crude loaded at the Turkish port of Ceyhan to take account of higher freight costs of 25-30 cents a barrel for shipping the barrels to destinations in northern Europe.
"The fact that they're still talking about it suggests SOMO is sympathetic to the idea," said a trader.
With world oil prices shedding over about $3 a barrel in the last three weeks, SOMO will have to find new customers and may have little choice but to offer better terms.
"Brent is at the lowest level for three months and it looks like we're in a low price environment so they will definitely need to pump more," said a trader.
Exports of Kirkuk and Basrah, loaded from the Gulf terminal of Mina al-Bakr, might need to rise to some to 750,000-800,000 barrels per day (bpd) to raise Iraq's permitted $2 billion limit.
Sales averaged 660,000 bpd in the first six-month wave which began in mid-December.

Any alterations to the original contracts, including adjustments to volume, destination or price, would require companies to send representatives to Baghdad to ink the new terms before submission to the U.N., a process which will inevitably delay exports.

"Certainly by the end of the week a few things will be signed but I don't see anything getting U.N. approval before next Monday. There may be nothing shipped in June except for Turkey," said a trader.

Husamettin Danis, general manager of Turkish state oil refiner Tupras which bought about 75,000 barrels per day (bpd) during the first six month period of the humanitarian deal, said Turkey's arrangement would be renewed but he could not give details about volumes.
SOMO is expected to settle price and volume terms this week, with Russian companies in pole position to take another big chunk of Iraqi exports.
Russian companies bought nearly 28.54 million barrels of oil under the first 180-day programme, 23.4 percent of the 121 million barrels Baghdad was permitted to export.
Yuri Agababov, deputy general director of Zarubezhneft, the Moscow-based firm coordinating Russian contracts, is leading a delegation to Iraq this week with the aim of securing similar volumes.
